reading_comprehension_tests.excerpt:
Humpty Dumpty sat on a wall,
Humpty Dumpty had a great fall.
All the king’s horses and all the king’s men,
Couldn’t put Humpty together again.

questions.question_text: Where did Humpty Dumpty sit?

options.A: In a green tree
options.B: On a high wall
options.C: On a small chair
options.D: In a deep hole

questions.explanation: The text directly states that 'Humpty Dumpty sat on a wall.'

questions.question_text: What happened to Humpty Dumpty?

options.A: He fell down
options.B: He went to sleep
options.C: He ran away
options.D: He sang a song

questions.explanation: The text states that he 'had a great fall,' meaning he fell down.

questions.question_text: Who came to try and help Humpty Dumpty?

options.A: Some little birds
options.B: The king's horses and men
options.C: A friendly farmer
options.D: His mother and father

questions.explanation: The rhyme notes that 'All the king’s horses and all the king’s men' arrived to assist.

questions.question_text: How does the story end for Humpty Dumpty?

options.A: He was fixed and went home
options.B: He climbed back up the wall
options.C: They could not put him together again
options.D: He walked away down the road

questions.explanation: The final line states they 'Couldn’t put Humpty together again.'

reading_comprehension_tests.excerpt: Flopsy, Mopsy, and Cotton-tail, who were good little bunnies, went down the lane to gather blackberries: But Peter, who was very naughty, ran straight away to Mr. McGregor's garden, and squeezed under the gate!

questions.question_text: What did Flopsy, Mopsy, and Cotton-tail go to gather?

options.A: Sweet red apples
options.B: Fresh green lettuce
options.C: Dark blackberries
options.D: Small brown nuts

questions.explanation: The text states the good little bunnies went 'to gather blackberries.'

questions.question_text: Where did Peter go instead of following his sisters?

options.A: Into the deep woods
options.B: To the baker's shop
options.C: Into Mr. McGregor's garden
options.D: Down to the running river

questions.explanation: Peter disobeyed and 'ran straight away to Mr. McGregor's garden.'

questions.question_text: How did Peter get inside the garden?

options.A: He jumped over the tall fence
options.B: He squeezed under the gate
options.C: He walked through the open door
options.D: He dug a hole in the dirt

questions.explanation: The passage states that Peter 'squeezed under the gate!'

questions.question_text: Why does the author call Peter 'naughty'?

options.A: Because he did not share his food
options.B: Because he went where he was told not to go
options.C: Because he fell asleep in the grass
options.D: Because he ran too fast for his sisters

questions.explanation: Peter is considered naughty because he runs off to the forbidden garden instead of gathering berries safely with his sisters.

reading_comprehension_tests.excerpt: The Tortoise never for a moment stopped, but went on with a slow but steady pace straight to the end of the course. The Hare, knowing himself to be fast, lay down by the wayside and fell fast asleep. At last waking up, he ran as fast as he could, but saw the Tortoise had already won the race.

questions.question_text: What did the Hare do because he knew he was fast?

options.A: He ran backward to show off
options.B: He stopped to eat lunch
options.C: He lay down and fell fast asleep
options.D: He helped the Tortoise walk

questions.explanation: Overconfident in his speed, the Hare 'lay down by the wayside and fell fast asleep.'

questions.question_text: How did the Tortoise move during the race?

options.A: He ran in quick bursts
options.B: He stopped many times to rest
options.C: He moved with a slow but steady pace
options.D: He followed behind the Hare closely

questions.explanation: The passage highlights that the Tortoise 'went on with a slow but steady pace.'

questions.question_text: What did the Hare see when he finally woke up?

options.A: The Tortoise had already won the race
options.B: The sun was just starting to rise
options.C: The Fox was waiting to start the race
options.D: The Tortoise was sleeping next to him

questions.explanation: Upon waking and running to the finish, the Hare 'saw the Tortoise had already won the race.'

questions.question_text: What is the main lesson of this story?

options.A: It is best to be as fast as possible
options.B: Staying steady and not quitting can lead to success
options.C: Racing against friends is dangerous
options.D: Sleeping during the day makes you run faster

questions.explanation: The narrative teaches that a persistent, steady effort ('slow and steady') triumphs over arrogance and lack of focus.

reading_comprehension_tests.excerpt: Mrs. Darling screamed, and, as if in answer to a bell, Nana entered the nursery. She growled and sprang at the boy, who leapt lightly through the window. Again Mrs. Darling screamed, this time in distress for him, for she thought he was killed, and she ran down into the street to look for his little body, but it was not there; and she looked up, and in the black night she could see nothing but what looked like a shooting star.

questions.question_text: How did the unknown boy escape from the nursery?

options.A: He hid inside a large closet
options.B: He ran past Nana out the front door
options.C: He leapt lightly out of the window
options.D: He climbed up into the chimney

questions.explanation: The text states the boy 'leapt lightly through the window' to escape Nana.

questions.question_text: Why did Mrs. Darling scream a second time?

options.A: She was terrified of her dog Nana
options.B: She feared the boy had fallen to his death
options.C: She realized her children were missing
options.D: She saw a ghost in the black night

questions.explanation: Her second scream was 'in distress for him, for she thought he was killed' by falling out the high window.

questions.question_text: What did Mrs. Darling find when she ran down into the street?

options.A: The boy waiting for her on the sidewalk
options.B: A broken window pane on the ground
options.C: Nothing at all where she thought he fell
options.D: Nana barking at a stranger

questions.explanation: When she arrived in the street to check for a body, the text states 'but it was not there.'

questions.question_text: What did the object in the sky look like to Mrs. Darling?

options.A: A bright full moon
options.B: A dark storm cloud
options.C: A large bird flying away
options.D: A shooting star

questions.explanation: Looking up into the dark sky, she saw 'nothing but what looked like a shooting star.'

reading_comprehension_tests.excerpt: She had a little thin face, a little thin body, thin light hair and a sour expression. Her hair was yellow, and her face was yellow because she had been born in India and had always been ill in one way or another. Her father had held a position under the English Government and had always been busy and ill himself, and her mother had been a great beauty who cared only to go to parties and amuse herself.

questions.question_text: According to the passage, why is Mary's face yellow?

options.A: She spent too many hours playing in the bright sun
options.B: She was born in India and was constantly sick
options.C: She was wearing a yellow hat that cast a shadow
options.D: She had a naturally cheerful and bright personality

questions.explanation: The text explicitly connects her yellow appearance to being 'born in India and had always been ill.'

questions.question_text: How does the author describe Mary’s mother?

options.A: As a hardworking woman who loved her home
options.B: As a sickly person who stayed in bed all day
options.C: As a great beauty who loved parties and amusement
options.D: As a strict teacher who made Mary study constantly

questions.explanation: Her mother is described as a 'great beauty who cared only to go to parties and amuse herself.'

questions.question_text: What do Mary and her father have in common?

options.A: They both loved to attend parties
options.B: They both suffered from frequent illness
options.C: They both worked for the English government
options.D: They both had thick, dark hair

questions.explanation: The text indicates Mary was 'always been ill' and her father was 'always been busy and ill himself.'

questions.question_text: What does the phrase 'sour expression' tell us about Mary?

options.A: She looked unhappy or unfriendly
options.B: She smelled like sour fruit
options.C: She was always tasting lemons
options.D: She had a very round, soft face

questions.explanation: A 'sour expression' is a physical description indicating a grumpy, unhappy, or cross facial expression.

reading_comprehension_tests.excerpt: The first place that I can well remember was a large pleasant meadow with a pond of clear water in it. Some shady trees leaned over it, and rushes and water-lilies grew at the deep end. Over the hedge on one side we looked into a plowed field, and on the other we looked over a gate at our master's house, which stood by the roadside. At the top of the meadow was a grove of fir trees, and at the bottom a running brook overhung by a steep bank.

questions.question_text: What perspective is this story narrated from?

options.A: A human master looking out at his property
options.B: An animal describing its early home environment
options.C: A visitor traveling down a rural roadside
options.D: A farmer working inside a plowed field

questions.explanation: The focus on the meadow lifestyle combined with referencing a 'master' implicitly signals an animal narrator (a horse) reflecting on early life.

questions.question_text: What can be found growing at the deep end of the pond?

options.A: Fir trees and tall pines
options.B: Rushes and water-lilies
options.C: Green grass and wild clover
options.D: Thick moss and heavy vines

questions.explanation: The text plainly reads that 'rushes and water-lilies grew at the deep end' of the pond.

questions.question_text: What boundary separates the meadow from the master's house?

options.A: A running brook with a steep bank
options.B: A thick grove of fir trees
options.C: A gate that looks over the roadside
options.D: A large patch of plowed earth

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that on one side 'we looked over a gate at our master's house.'

questions.question_text: What is the overall tone established by this description of the setting?

options.A: Mysterious and frightening
options.B: Peaceful and comfortable
options.C: Busy and industrial
options.D: Lonely and neglected

questions.explanation: Words like 'pleasant meadow,' 'clear water,' 'shady trees,' and a running brook cultivate a serene and comforting mood.

reading_comprehension_tests.excerpt: Tom appeared on the sidewalk with a bucket of whitewash and a long-handled brush. He surveyed the fence, and all gladness departed from him and a deep melancholy settled down upon his spirit. Thirty yards of board fence nine feet high. It seemed to him that life was hollow, and existence but a burden. Sighing, he dipped his brush and passed it along the topmost plank...

questions.question_text: How does Tom feel when he looks at the fence he must paint?

options.A: Excited to show off his painting skills
options.B: Deeply sad and completely discouraged
options.C: Annoyed that the brush is broken
options.D: Eager to finish so he can go swimming

questions.explanation: The text states that 'all gladness departed from him' and he felt life was a burden, showing heavy discouragement.

questions.question_text: What does the word 'melancholy' mean as used in this passage?

options.A: Extreme anger
options.B: Great sorrow or gloom
options.C: Sudden excitement
options.D: Deep confusion

questions.explanation: Melancholy describes a state of deep, persistent sadness or low spirits, matching Tom's outlook on his chore.

questions.question_text: What is the physical scale of the task Tom is facing?

options.A: A small garden gate near the sidewalk
options.B: A few broken boards on a short wall
options.C: Thirty yards of fence that stands nine feet high
options.D: An entire house that needs multiple coats of paint

questions.explanation: The author provides exact measurements: 'Thirty yards of board fence nine feet high.'

questions.question_text: Why does Tom feel that 'life was hollow'?

options.A: He has no friends to play with on the weekend
options.B: He feels overwhelmed by the chore assigned to him
options.C: He lost his favorite bucket and long-handled brush
options.D: He is feeling very sick from working out in the sun

questions.explanation: The dread of the immense physical task ahead makes his day feel entirely devoid of joy, making life seem 'hollow.'

reading_comprehension_tests.excerpt: I remember him as if it were yesterday, as he came plodding to the inn door, his sea-chest following behind him in a hand-barrow—a tall, strong, heavy, nut-brown man, his tarry pigtail falling over the shoulder of his soiled blue coat, his hands ragged and scarred, with black, broken nails, and the sabre-cut across one cheek, a dirty, livid white.

questions.question_text: Which detail best indicates that the newcomer has lived a rugged or violent life?

options.A: He arrived at the inn door with a hand-barrow
options.B: He wore a blue coat that was heavily soiled
options.C: He had ragged, scarred hands and a sabre-cut on his cheek
options.D: He had a long pigtail falling over his shoulder

questions.explanation: Scars, rugged hands, and specifically a weapon-inflicted 'sabre-cut' characterize physical conflict and heavy, rough physical labor.

questions.question_text: What does the word 'plodding' suggest about how the man walked?

options.A: Running quickly to escape danger
options.B: Walking slowly and heavily with great effort
options.C: Skipping cheerfully toward the inn entrance
options.D: Marching precisely like a trained soldier

questions.explanation: 'Plodding' means to trudge or walk with slow, heavy steps, conveying exhaustion or the physical weight of his journey.

questions.question_text: What color is the scar on the man's cheek described as?

options.A: Nut-brown
options.B: Dark blue
options.C: Tarry black
options.D: Livid white

questions.explanation: The text tracks the scar explicitly, noting 'the sabre-cut across one cheek, a dirty, livid white.'

questions.question_text: How does the narrator characterize this memory?

options.A: As a blurry event that is difficult to recall
options.B: As a frightening dream from childhood
options.C: As an incredibly sharp, clear, and lasting image
options.D: As a funny story told to him by his parents

questions.explanation: The opening phrase 'I remember him as if it were yesterday' underscores a persistent, highly detailed memory.

reading_comprehension_tests.excerpt: Dark spruce forest frowned on either side the frozen waterway. The trees had been stripped by a recent wind of their white covering of frost, and they seemed to lean toward each other, black and ominous, in the fading light. A vast silence reigned over the land. The land itself was a desolation, lifeless, without movement, so lone and cold that its spirit was not even that of sadness.

questions.question_text: What has caused the trees to lose their frost covering?

options.A: The intense heat of the afternoon sun
options.B: A recent wind that stripped the branches
options.C: A sudden downpour of freezing rain
options.D: The heavy weight of native wildlife

questions.explanation: The text documents that 'The trees had been stripped by a recent wind of their white covering.'

questions.question_text: How does the author personify the spruce forest?

options.A: By describing it as sleeping peacefully
options.B: By stating that it frowned on either side
options.C: By depicting it as reaching out to help
options.D: By showing it laughing in the dark

questions.explanation: Giving human actions to nature, the text writes that the 'spruce forest frowned.'

questions.question_text: What does the word 'ominous' mean in the context of this passage?

options.A: Bright and welcoming
options.B: Giving the impression that something bad will happen
options.C: Ancient and wise
options.D: Quiet and completely harmless

questions.explanation: 'Ominous' stems from omen, suggesting a threatening, menacing presence indicating future danger or doom.

questions.question_text: What is unique about the 'spirit' of this landscape?

options.A: It is filled with a deep, tragic human sorrow
options.B: It is so intensely cold and desolate that it goes beyond mere sadness
options.C: It changes rapidly whenever the wind blows
options.D: It brings a feeling of comfort and safety to travelers

questions.explanation: The text describes it as 'so lone and cold that its spirit was not even that of sadness,' pointing to an unfeeling, transcendent emptiness.

reading_comprehension_tests.excerpt: Tell me, O Muse, of that ingenious hero who travelled far and wide after he had sacked the famous town of Troy. Many cities did he visit, and many were the nations with whose manners and customs he was acquainted; moreover he suffered much by sea while trying to save his own life and bring his men safely home; but do what he might he could not save his men, for they perished through their own sheer folly...

questions.question_text: What adjective does the translator use to describe the central hero?

options.A: Famous
options.B: Ingenious
options.C: Safe
options.D: Perished

questions.explanation: The text introduces the main subject explicitly as 'that ingenious hero.'

questions.question_text: What was the primary goal of the hero during his sea travels?

options.A: To conquer new cities and build an empire
options.B: To learn the secrets and languages of the Muses
options.C: To protect his own life and return his crew safely home
options.D: To find gold hidden away in the ruins of Troy

questions.explanation: The narrator states he was 'trying to save his own life and bring his men safely home.'

questions.question_text: According to the narrator, why did the hero's men lose their lives?

options.A: Because the hero made a series of terrible mistakes
options.B: Because of their own foolish actions and choices
options.C: Because a violent storm destroyed their fleet
options.D: Because the gods were angry at the fall of Troy

questions.explanation: The text states the crew 'perished through their own sheer folly,' with folly indicating foolishness or lack of sense.

questions.question_text: What does the passage imply about the hero's experience?

options.A: It was a short, easy journey across familiar lands
options.B: It was a deeply educational but physically agonizing ordeal
options.C: It was a failed mission that ended in total obscurity
options.D: It was entirely planned and directed by his soldiers

questions.explanation: The narrator notes he became acquainted with many customs ('educational') yet 'suffered much by sea' ('agonizing').

metadata.author: Jack London
metadata.focus_standard: Authorial Intent, Irony, and Historical Setting Context

reading_comprehension_tests.excerpt: Buck did not read the newspapers, or he would have known that trouble was brewing, not alone for himself, but for every tide-water dog, strong of muscle and with warm, long hair, from Puget Sound to San Diego. Because men, groping in the Arctic darkness, had found a yellow metal, and because steamship and transportation companies were booming the find, thousands of men were rushing into the Northland. These men wanted dogs, and the dogs they wanted were heavy dogs, with strong muscles by which to toil, and furry coats to protect them from the frost.

questions.question_text: What structural irony opens this passage?

options.A: Buck knows about the gold rush but chooses to ignore it
options.B: Men are searching for dogs but cannot find any near Puget Sound
options.C: Buck's safety is threatened by global events he cannot read about
options.D: The shipping companies are going bankrupt due to the cold weather

questions.explanation: The irony lies in the fact that Buck is a dog whose life is about to change drastically due to human political/economic movements documented in media he is biologically incapable of reading.

questions.question_text: What discovery triggered the massive rush of people into the Northland?

options.A: A new shipping route through San Diego
options.B: A valuable yellow metal found in the Arctic darkness
options.C: A rare breed of long-haired tide-water dogs
options.D: An abundance of lumber in the spruce forests

questions.explanation: The rush began because 'men, groping in the Arctic darkness, had found a yellow metal' (gold).

questions.question_text: What specific physical traits make a dog valuable to the men rushing north?

options.A: Speed, agility, and a quiet demeanor
options.B: Small size, high intelligence, and tracking skills
options.C: Strong muscles for heavy labor and a warm, furry coat
options.D: Aggression, sharp vision, and loyalty to one master

questions.explanation: The text explicitly states they required 'heavy dogs, with strong muscles by which to toil, and furry coats to protect them from the frost.'

questions.question_text: What does the word 'groping' imply about the men searching for gold?

options.A: They were working blindly or with great difficulty in harsh conditions
options.B: They were celebrating their sudden and easy wealth
options.C: They were carefully charting maps for future generations
options.D: They were destroying the local environment out of anger

questions.explanation: 'Groping' in 'darkness' suggests searching uncertainly, feeling around blindly, and working through immense systemic difficulty.

metadata.author: F. Scott Fitzgerald
metadata.focus_standard: Subtext Analysis, Idiomatic Phrases, and Philosophical Frameworks

reading_comprehension_tests.excerpt: In my younger and more vulnerable years my father gave some advice that I’ve been turning over in my mind ever since. "Whenever you feel like criticizing any one," he told me, "just remember that all the people in this world haven’t had the advantages that you’ve had." He didn’t say any more, but we’ve always been unusually communicative in a reserved way, and I understood that he meant a great deal more than that. In consequence, I’m inclined to reserve all judgments...

questions.question_text: What core principle underlies the advice given by the narrator's father?

options.A: Social class distinctions are permanent and should be respected
options.B: Personal fortune and privilege are unequally distributed across society
options.C: Expressing direct criticism is essential for effective communication
options.D: Family loyalty must supersede all commitments to outside individuals

questions.explanation: The statement about others not having 'the advantages that you’ve had' reminds the narrator that privilege is not universally distributed.

questions.question_text: What paradox does the narrator use to describe his relationship with his father?

options.A: They were completely distant yet lived in the same household
options.B: They spoke constantly but never truly understood one another
options.C: They were unusually communicative while remaining reserved
options.D: They agreed on philosophical matters but disagreed on politics

questions.explanation: The text explicitly states: 'we’ve always been unusually communicative in a reserved way.'

questions.question_text: What personal behavioral trait develops as a direct result of this parental advice?

options.A: A tendency to avoid social interactions entirely
options.B: A habit of holding back personal moral condemnation of others
options.C: A desire to pursue positions of high political power
options.D: An obsession with tracking the financial success of his peers

questions.explanation: Because of the advice, the narrator says, 'In consequence, I’m inclined to reserve all judgments.'

questions.question_text: In this context, what does the phrase 'turning over in my mind' mean?

options.A: Forgetting a memory over a long period of time
options.B: Actively debating whether an idea is factually correct
options.C: Constantly reflecting on and analyzing an concept
options.D: Regretting an action taken during youth

questions.explanation: To 'turn something over' in one's mind is a common idiom meaning to evaluate, think deeply about, or continuously reflect on an idea.

metadata.author: Mary Shelley
metadata.focus_standard: High-Level Genre Analysis (Gothicism), Syntax, and Thematic Shifts

reading_comprehension_tests.excerpt: It was on a dreary night of November that I beheld the accomplishment of my toils. With an anxiety that almost amounted to agony, I collected the instruments of life around me, that I might infuse a spark of being into the lifeless thing that lay at my feet. It was already one in the morning; the rain pattered dismally against the panes, and my candle was nearly burnt out, when, by the glimmer of the half-extinguished light, I saw the dull yellow eye of the creature open; it breathed hard, and a convulsive motion agitated its limbs.

questions.question_text: How does the author utilize Gothic imagery to frame the structural climax of creation?

options.A: By contrasting scientific progress with a warm, comforting domestic hearth
options.B: By setting the event at midnight during a vibrant summer thunderstorm
options.C: By combining a dying candle, dismal rain, and a dreary November night to mirror psychological dread
options.D: By emphasizing the sterile, brightly lit, and highly ordered space of a modern laboratory

questions.explanation: Shelley coordinates classic Gothic tropes (rainy dark night, burnout candle, dark room) to construct an external parallel to Victor's psychological anxiety.

questions.question_text: What profound psychological shift does the narrator experience at the moment of success?

options.A: A transition from intellectual passion to immediate existential agony and horror
options.B: A surge of supreme confidence and pride in his absolute triumph over mortality
options.C: A feeling of profound boredom and indifference toward his completed work
options.D: Sudden religious enlightenment that causes him to destroy his laboratory instruments

questions.explanation: The text balances his dynamic pursuit against 'an anxiety that almost amounted to agony' immediately as the unnatural creature opens its eye.

questions.question_text: What physical details signal that the animation of the creature is incomplete or unnatural?

options.A: The creature begins to speak fluent, complex philosophical arguments
options.B: A convulsive motion agitates its limbs as its dull yellow eye opens
options.C: The creature immediately stands up and flees into the pouring rain
options.D: It remains completely motionless despite the spark of being infused into it

questions.explanation: The creature’s life is marked explicitly by a 'dull yellow eye' opening and 'a convulsive motion' disrupting its limbs, rather than a smooth, natural awakening.

questions.question_text: What does the phrase 'accomplishment of my toils' signify textually?

options.A: The failure of a long-term economic investment
options.B: The structural beginning of a peaceful new career phase
options.C: The physical manifestation and culmination of intense, exhausting labor
options.D: The destruction of historical instruments used in traditional medicine

questions.explanation: 'Toils' references exhaustive, challenging physical and mental labor; the 'accomplishment' means that work has finally yielded its physical goal.
